evidence.text: The database indexes oracle-bone forms, including 合集9748, bronze forms including 集成09898, Chu manuscripts, and seal-script/Shuowen forms. Its account identifies the graph’s basic conception as two people facing away from one another, while the displayed text does not provide a dated sequence of form-by-form changes.
evidence.title: 漢字「北」：字形演變

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The author says the two-back-to-back-person conception remains clear from Shang writing through the Shuowen seal form, with changes in writing strokes rather than conception. Cited examples include oracle-bone inscriptions 合集6057 and 29401, Shang bronze 集成2710, Western Zhou bronzes 集成2804 and 2819, Chu slips, and Qin slips. The author proposes the graph’s original use was ‘turn against/back on’ or ‘defy’; this graphic interpretation does not by itself date or prove that word sense.
evidence.title: “北”字职用演变研究（一）

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study says 北 was used as a phonetic loan for the direction ‘north’ from the Shang period, and that this use continued as its principal function. It explicitly says it cannot identify secure excavated examples of 北 writing the hypothesized original ‘turn against/back’ sense; that inference is based on the graphic account and related later uses. The study traces proposed extensions from turning against to back of the body, back side, facing with one’s back, concealment, betrayal, abandonment, military flight/defeat, and defeated troops. It gives Qin-Han manuscript examples for ‘back’ and ‘back side,’ and examples from transmitted texts and excavated manuscripts for betrayal, abandonment, and defeat. These are an author’s semantic analysis; the attestation order should not be read as a complete chronology of spoken senses.
evidence.title: “北”字职用演变研究（一）

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study dates the differentiation of 背 with the 肉 semantic element and 北 as phonetic to around the Qin-Han transition, citing an early Western Han Zhangjiashan manuscript example in 引书. It reports 北 still commonly wrote the ‘back’ word in that corpus, while 背 became the usual graph by the Eastern Han, supported by an Eastern Han Wuwei medical manuscript and the Shuowen definition of 背 as ‘spine/back.’ This describes graph differentiation, not proof that the word ‘back’ first arose then.
evidence.title: “北”字职用演变研究（一）

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study separately states that 北 was used from Shang times as a loan graph for ‘north,’ and that it also recorded names associated with the north and other words such as ‘separate’ and ‘lowly’ in later periods. It distinguishes these borrowed uses from proposed semantic extensions of the original back/turning-against word. It also discusses some later graph confusions as copying or printing errors rather than part of 北’s etymological functions.
evidence.title: “北”字职用演变研究（三）

evidence.source: Xu Shen, Shuowen Jiezi, text hosted by Wikisource
evidence.text: The Han dictionary entry reads 北：𦮃也。從二人相背。凡北之屬皆從北。 It gives a gloss conventionally understood as ‘turning away/contrary’ and analyzes the graph as two people back-to-back. This is an ancient lexicographic account, not independent confirmation of the graph’s first use.
evidence.title: 說文解字/08

evidence.source: University of Cambridge? Laurent Sagart, The Chinese names of the four directions, hosted by vLex
evidence.text: Sagart reports the four direction graphs are attested in Shang epigraphy, and proposes a lexical relation between north and ‘the back’: an Old Chinese root meaning ‘turn the back’ developed into north and a body-part noun with a nominalizing suffix. He considers south a likely direction of reference, based on later evidence such as south-oriented compasses and maps, while explicitly acknowledging that those facts are later than the proposed Shang setting. This is a linguistic proposal and does not independently establish that the semantic transition occurred in that exact sequence.
evidence.title: The Chinese names of the four directions

evidence.text: The Guangyun record gives 北 the fanqie 博墨切, labial initial, open first division, 德 rhyme, entering tone; several listed reconstruction columns give pək, and Baxter’s Middle Chinese notation gives pok. This is a medieval rhyme-dictionary record, not direct Shang pronunciation evidence.

gaps: No primary oracle-bone inscription image or full inscription context was inspected in this research. The Academia Sinica database lists catalogued forms, while the Zhengzhou University study supplies the cited inscription identifiers and its author’s reading.

The proposed original back-related sense is not securely attested in the excavated records surveyed by the paleographic study; the author infers it from graphic form and later related uses. The graph is already used for ‘north’ in Shang-period evidence, so chronology of the spoken meanings is not established merely by the sequence of glosses.

The ‘north’ loan explanation is supported by the reported Shang use and distinct back-to-back graphic analysis, but no specific source-word/object reading is recoverable or needed as an object name; the proposed lexical relation remains an etymological account rather than direct proof of a borrowing event.

The source study presents ‘back/turn against’ extensions as connected senses, but dates only some written attestations and explicitly notes uncertainty or lack of examples for several proposed early uses. Semantic links and exact chronology remain partly inferential.

The search result for the Baxter-Sagart 北 module could not be opened due to a cache miss; its result was not treated as inspected page evidence. The accessible Chinese phonology compilation reports the same reconstruction.

No independent evidence was found to establish why individual modern Japanese, Korean, or Cantonese readings developed as they did; the modern readings are included only as contemporary pronunciation data.
